title: Trace
summary: A debug console for finding the bad records hiding in ML training data.

meta.label: TOOLS
meta.value: Figma, plus a working console in React and TypeScript

blocks.text: A model is only as good as the data it trains on. When a few records are broken, like an empty label or an impossible image size, the training run fails or, worse, quietly learns the wrong thing.
The people who deal with that are ML and data engineers. In that moment their job is detective work: which records are bad, why, and what is safe to do about them.

Trace is the tool I would want open then. I designed it around one made-up batch from a self-driving camera dataset: 48 records, 36 pass, 8 are invalid and block training, 4 have warnings. All of the data is synthetic and the assistant is simulated. The product says so on screen.

I got curious about what happens before a model ever trains. Reading about how self-driving teams clean their camera annotations, I learned that one bad label can block a whole batch, and the people fixing it often dig through logs and spreadsheets. I wanted to design the tool I would want open in that moment.
Trace is a desktop console with one job: get you from "this batch failed" to "this batch is ready to train" without losing any data on the way.

blocks.caption: 12 seconds. Filter the invalid records, select them, quarantine, revalidate, and land on "Passed with warnings".
Batch 024 on the dataset screen: the health summary and rule outcomes.

blocks.text: You start on a health summary, then work through a table you can search and filter. Opening a record shows the problem in plain words, the rule it broke, and the raw JSON. A Batch assistant tab explains why the batch failed and links to the evidence.
I drew the unglamorous screens too: empty results, loading, validation running, and failure with retry. In total that is 31 desktop screens, a 12-screen mobile prototype, and 7 prototype flows.
When you find a broken record, the quick fix is to delete it. Then the evidence is gone. Nobody can audit it later, and a mistake made in a hurry cannot be undone.

So Trace moves records aside instead. A quarantined record is left out of training but kept exactly as it was, with its raw JSON still there to read. Restoring one is not taken on trust either. Trace runs validation again first.

frames.caption: Eight records quarantined, batch waiting on revalidation.
Restore a record that is still broken and the batch still blocks.

blocks.text: Designing that last screen, where restoring does not fix it, is when the rule stopped being a nice sentence and became real.

blocks.title: The assistant explains. It never edits.

blocks.text: An assistant that can "fix the batch" demos well. In a training pipeline a confident wrong fix is worse than no fix, because nobody notices it.

So the assistant only explains. It sums up the problem ("8 records are blocking this batch") and groups the evidence: 5 missing labels, 3 invalid dimensions, 2 duplicates, 2 low resolution. Each group links to the records behind it. The panel is labeled "Simulated AI, rule-based", and its footer says suggestions never change records.

blocks.caption: When the assistant fails, it says so and tells you your records and validation results are unchanged.

blocks.text: I wanted it to make people faster at understanding, not to make decisions for them. Labeling it honestly was part of the design from the start.

blocks.title: Looking at a record is not choosing it

blocks.text: In most tables, clicking a row opens it and selects it. That is fine until the main action is "quarantine selected." You can be reading one record and act on it by accident.

In Trace the highlighted row is what you are inspecting, and the checkboxes are what you have selected. The bulk bar says exactly what a button will touch: "8 selected, Quarantine, Restore, Clear selection."

blocks.caption: Eight records selected while the inspector still shows rec_01284.

blocks.text: Separating the two makes the bulk action predictable. You always know what a button will touch.

items.title: Rules first, screens second.
items.text: I wrote three plain rules before drawing much: quarantine preserves, AI never mutates, looking is not choosing. When I was unsure what a screen should do, I checked it against them.

items.title: The best screen is the one where the user is wrong.
items.text: The restored record that still blocks the batch taught me more than the happy path did.

items.title: A brand color has to earn its place.
items.text: The green I wanted is 2.41:1 on white, too weak for text. It became a surface, with dark ink on top and darker greens wherever people have to read.

blocks.caption: Dataset overview, before and after the restyle.

blocks.text: Trace has not been tested with real users yet. The prototype says so itself: "Synthetic data, simulated AI, user interviews and usability sessions still to be conducted."

items.text: Interview five ML or data engineers about how they find bad records today.
Run usability sessions on the quarantine and restore flow.
Connect the console to a real public dataset instead of synthetic records.
